items.title: Every Sikh gurdwara serves a free meal to all visitors

options.text: A meal sold to support the gurdwara

A free communal meal served to anyone regardless of religion, caste, gender or background — a foundational Sikh practice, originated by Guru Nanak, institutionalised by Guru Amar Das (3rd Guru) who required visitors to eat langar before meeting him
A meal restricted to initiated Khalsa Sikhs

items.reveal:
Langar is served in the langar hall of every gurdwara worldwide. All sit on the floor at the same level to eat — explicitly rejecting caste hierarchy. The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar) serves around 100,000 meals daily; volunteers prepare and clean.

Guru Amar Das (1479-1574) made eating langar a requirement before meeting him — including for the Mughal Emperor Akbar, who reportedly sat with peasants before being granted an audience.

In the UK, Sikh organisations like Khalsa Aid extend the langar tradition to refugees, food banks and disaster response — recently in Ukraine, Turkey, and at UK floods.
items.why: Practice can teach doctrine. The simple physical act of sitting on the floor and eating together puts equality into the body — more direct than verbal teaching.

items.title: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible

options.text: The first five books — Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy — traditionally attributed to Moses; also called the Pentateuch or Chumash; the first section of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh)

items.reveal:
The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) is structured in three sections: Torah (Teaching, 5 books), Nevi'im (Prophets, 8 books in Jewish count), Ketuvim (Writings, 11 books). 'Tanakh' is an acronym of those three.

The Torah is read in synagogue in an annual cycle (some Reform congregations use a triennial cycle). The cycle ends and restarts on Simchat Torah.

The Written Torah is complemented by the Oral Torah — the rabbinic tradition codified in the Mishnah (around 200 CE) and Talmud (around 500 CE). For Orthodox Judaism, both were revealed at Sinai.
items.why: 'The Torah' is often used loosely. Students need to distinguish Torah (5 books) from Tanakh (24 books) from Talmud (rabbinic commentary) — and notice that the Christian Old Testament has the same content but in different order.

items.title: Moral and natural evil are distinct problems for theism
items.claim: What is the distinction between moral and natural evil?

options.text: All evil is caused by human moral failure

Moral evil is caused by free moral agents (murder, torture, cruelty); natural evil is caused by impersonal natural processes (earthquakes, disease, predation) — they raise different problems for theistic theodicies
Natural evil is just a subset of moral evil

items.reveal:
Free Will Defence (Augustine, Alvin Plantinga) explains moral evil as the cost of human free will — but doesn't obviously address natural evil. Earthquakes do not flow from human choices.

Irenaean theodicy (revived by John Hick, 'Evil and the God of Love', 1966) sees natural evil as part of soul-making — character development requires a challenging environment.

Augustinian theodicy treats evil as privatio boni (privation of good) — not a substance but an absence. The Fall extends moral consequences into nature.

The logical problem of evil (J. L. Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence', 1955) has been largely answered by Plantinga's free-will defence; the evidential problem (William Rowe, 1979) remains live.
items.why: The problem of evil is the most persistent challenge to classical theism. The moral/natural and logical/evidential distinctions shape which theodicies are even relevant — generic answers miss the structure of the argument.
